talks.title: What to Expect in the Call That You Do Not Want to Be Part Of
talks.teaser: A session outlines the first incident call after ransomware or business email compromise, from insurance through forensics and recovery.
talks.summary:
Organizations that discover ransomware or business email compromise face a stressful first coordination call that must serve two goals at once: restoring operations and preserving a defensible investigation. The presenters frame both attack types as financially motivated threats that hit businesses of any size, with examples including large spoofed payment redirects and six-figure church fundraiser losses. They stress knowing cyber insurance contacts early, understanding first- and third-party coverage, typical policy pricing for smaller firms, and exclusions such as intentional acts, infrastructure outages, and weak security practices.

Much of the material mirrors what counsel and digital forensics consultants ask on that initial call: what happened in the victim’s words, timelines, suspected entry points, crown jewels, regulated or contractual data, environment scale and normality, remote access and MFA gaps, and whether backups exist, were tested, and remain safe from the attacker. The discussion covers engaging threat actors when needed, OFAC considerations, FBI guidance tensions, and follow-on data theft extortion. Field stories highlight missing data inventories, failed backups, and translation quirks in ransom chats.

Closing guidance targets small and medium businesses: employee and vendor training, phishing drills, printed offline incident plans with current contacts, risk assessments, encryption and 3-2-1 backups, least-privilege access, client notification planning, and overlapping recovery with imaging of systems that matter for regulatory reporting while clearing less critical endpoints when appropriate.

talks.title: Security Career Development Planning
talks.teaser: Shares a career path into security leadership, with advice on pay, well-being, certifications and building professional networks.
talks.summary:
The speaker walks through his own career, starting with early jobs in roofing and retail, moving into IT data administration, and then into compliance work after his employer was acquired by a larger equipment company. He explains that promotions and pay depend on showing your value and speaking up for yourself, since waiting to be noticed did not work for him.

The middle of the talk covers personal well-being and compensation. He describes working very long hours, then setting boundaries on after-hours calls, and treats fitness, hobbies and social connection as parts of a sustainable growth plan. For pay, he recommends researching rates for your role and region through salary sites, peers and conferences, weighing local cost of living, and negotiating calmly instead of issuing an ultimatum. He also compares the individual contributor, consultant and leadership tracks, noting that delegation is hard for experts and that subject-matter experts must learn to communicate and sell their services.

He closes with certifications as a way to show credibility, while acknowledging that the options are long and expensive. He urges people to keep up with industry change, document processes, volunteer for projects and build networks of trust. He points to a flood of applicants for one local CISO posting as a sign of a competitive market, and encourages mentoring and outreach to students and youth groups to grow future talent.

talks.title: CypherCon 6 Closing Ceremony
talks.teaser: Wraps up CypherCon 6 by recapping its village contests, badge hacks, a charity auction and next year's plans.
talks.summary:
The CypherCon 6 closing ceremony recaps the week's contests, village challenges and badge hacks. In Wi-Fi King of the Hill, five DJs competed for the crown and one kept it for roughly four hours, while a fox-hunting contest saw one player locate four foxes. Hungry Hungry Hackers qualifiers left only five people on the board, so organizers ran walkthrough demos and then a live head-to-head round that a player won. In the AI village, a bot puzzle asked participants to manipulate its responses, and one student solved it in three queries.

Other challenges included the ISP village, where a cable modem was the entry point to pivot upstream through successive devices, a path that took one winner about six hours. The IoT village ran a nine-device capture-the-flag, won by a student team. The Espionage village released 20 puzzle packets, and six teams finished. The Cipher Cube puzzle box was auctioned for charity and sold for $700. Prizes for the cipher puzzle went to the fastest solvers, and the quickest finished in 17 minutes.

Badge and lock contests closed out the session. A safe-cracking challenge was won by a contestant who used roughly $3,000 of specialized tools, earning a lifetime badge. Last year's Flamingo badge had a credit-underflow flaw that let players create extra credits on other badges, and this year's winning team escaped a MicroPython browser sandbox. Closing announcements covered a November conference in Minnesota and CypherCon 7, themed as a casino heist, set for April 4 and 5.

talks.title: Break Time with Cortex, Palo Alto Networks
talks.teaser: Christine Konopka | CypherCon 6.0 investigates Break Time with Cortex, Palo Alto Networks.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Christine Kapka, a Cortex Systems Engineer at Palo Alto Networks, discusses how security operations teams can incorporate automation into their workflows using the Cortex XSOAR platform. Security Operations Centers (SOCs) face ongoing challenges such as alert overload, siloed tools, small team sizes, and the high time commitment required to investigate alerts manually. While automation is not a complete cure-all, Kapka demonstrates how XSOAR's playbooks and case management streamline alert triage, indicator enrichment, and repetitive tasks like routine vulnerability scan requests.

### Key Topics
- **SOC Challenges**: Teams struggle with excessive alert volumes, navigating disparate interfaces across siloed products, and spending excessive time on repetitive, manual tasks.
- **Indicator of Compromise (IOC) Enrichment**: Automated extraction and enrichment of indicators (IP addresses, URLs, hashes, and Active Directory user context) via modular playbooks and sub-playbooks.
- **End-to-End Phishing Incident Response**: Automating complex phishing workflows, from user acknowledgement and email rasterization to indicator detonation, inbox hunting, and blocking malicious entities.
- **Malware Investigation and Response**: Standardizing detection, indicator enrichment, analysis, and containment (such as endpoint isolation) across integrated tools.
- **Operational Metrics and SOC Sustainability**: Demonstrating measurable time savings and improving analyst retention and work-life balance.

### Technical Details
- **IOC Enrichment Workflow**: Kapka outlines a three-step model—Extract, Enrich, and Update. Alerts ingested from EDRs, SIEMs, or emails trigger playbooks that parse out IPs, hashes, and URLs. The playbook queries internal systems (DNS, Active Directory, endpoint tools) and external threat feeds (such as VirusTotal). If indicators are confirmed malicious, block lists and firewall watch lists are automatically updated; otherwise, the incident is closed or routed for analyst review.
- **Phishing Response Automation**: Standard phishing workflows typically span 10 to 12 steps. In XSOAR, playbooks ingest the alert, automatically email the reporting user, rasterize the email for visual review, and extract attributes. Attachments are detonated, reputations checked, and if found malicious, severity is escalated to critical. The system searches and purges the email across other organization mailboxes. While analysts can retain a manual confirmation step, investigation time drops from 40–45 minutes per alert down to seconds or minutes.
- **Malware Investigation Pack**: Addresses tool fragmentation across SIEM, EDR, and threat intelligence. Built to support solutions like Cortex XDR, CrowdStrike, and Microsoft, the pack automates queries and enables direct containment actions, such as isolating endpoints without leaving the XSOAR interface.
- **Real-World Impact and Internal Metrics**:
  - *Financial Services Customer*: Handled 730 phishing alerts per week; XSOAR automatically closed 430 due to deduplication and spam filtering, saving four analyst days per month on phishing alone.
  - *Palo Alto Networks Internal SOC*: Monitors 1.5 trillion events over 90 days across 10,000+ employees. XSOAR automated responses to 5,200 alerts, leaving only 800 requiring manual intervention.

### Takeaways
Automating repetitive tier-one tasks dramatically cuts response times, prevents analyst burnout, and supports staff retention. Palo Alto Networks leverages a "30-30-30" approach where analysts split time between alerts, investigations, and proactive projects, eliminating SOC turnover. Teams starting with automation can begin simply by centralizing case management and automating indicator enrichment to establish baseline metrics before expanding into automated containment.

talks.title: The dangers of online speech
talks.teaser: Explains how defamation and contract clauses can expose technologists to legal risk, and how to spot them early.
talks.summary:
Ken Vedaa, a lawyer working in incident response for a federal agency, begins by challenging the belief that free speech shields technologists from consequences. The First Amendment restricts only the government, so employers and individuals can still create legal exposure for online statements. Most trouble, he says, comes as either a defamation claim or a breach of a signed contract.

On defamation, he walks through the elements: a false factual statement, communication to a third party, fault such as negligence, and resulting harm. Accusing someone of a crime can count as defamation per se, which removes the need to prove damages. On contracts, he covers nondisclosure, severance, handbook, licensing and settlement agreements, and urges careful reading before signing. He notes a 2023 labor board ruling limiting severance clauses that bar discussing working conditions, though such rulings can shift. He also flags arbitration, which is closed to the public, along with non-compete and non-derogatory clauses. One case he cites involved over $400,000 in legal fees on a claim of $1 in damages.

He shares being sued for defamation over online comments from an online graduate program, a case that took years of trips to Massachusetts before summary judgment. He explains that long-arm statutes and data center locations can pull online speech into distant courts. He closes by urging people to review contracts early, negotiate limits while they have leverage, and remember that even dismissed suits cost time and money.

talks.title: Executives Overcoming the CyberSecurity Poverty Line Robert Wagner | CypherCon 6.0
talks.teaser: Gives executives at small organizations practical ways to build teams, prioritize controls and justify security budgets.
talks.summary:
Robert Wagner speaks to executives and newly promoted security managers at small and medium organizations that lack the budget for basic security. He builds on the idea of a cyber security poverty line, arguing that money is only part of the gap, with expertise, capability and influence also holding teams back. He notes that small and medium enterprises are a growing target, making up about 46% of attacks, and that many victims go out of business after a breach.

On people, he urges leaders to hire a strategic manager who speaks business language and treats audits as negotiations, instead of chasing an unrealistic unicorn. He describes a six-person team whose manager encouraged mentoring, and which outperformed a larger group that only ran tools. He suggests interns, rotating analysts through tasks instead of tier one, two and three structures to limit burnout, reworded job postings that focus on duties, blind resume review and structured interviews. Training should be regular and rewarded rather than punished, and it should apply to executives as well.

For process, he recommends starting with the CIS Controls implementation groups and prioritizing the controls that address the attacks hitting similar organizations, such as email and browsers. He criticizes risk matrices and suggests asking leadership for its risk appetite in dollar and probability terms, then using assessments as purple-team exercises with credentials provided. Practical moves include MFA for everyone, jump boxes, rotating hardened images and honey files, which can produce evidence to support a budget request.

talks.title: How to look good when followed by the FSB (KGB)
talks.teaser: Offers practical advice for security pros traveling abroad, covering border searches, device prep and blending in.
talks.summary:
The presenters, who describe travel as a family tradition, argue that security professionals abroad can draw attention simply by looking like one. They point to the main risks as customs and border agencies that can search devices and detain travelers, foreign services, and opportunistic criminal groups that may take an interest in visitors. Their stated goal is not to act like a spy but to avoid becoming a memorable target.

Much of the advice concerns preparation. Before a trip, they suggest deciding which accounts, admin rights and data are truly needed, using loaner or wiped devices, and writing down a check-in plan. Biometric unlock can be turned off so that a passcode must be given. Messaging apps should match what locals use, since some are blocked or draw scrutiny in certain countries. Burner phones bought with cash should be activated away from a main phone. In hotels, the speakers warn about cameras, staff monitoring and key cards that can be tracked, and recommend carrying a spare key and keeping devices close at all times.

The closing point is that secure travel is inconvenient, so practice matters. Clothing, shoes and even haircuts can reveal where someone is from, so travelers should dress in a way that does not stand out and avoid political discussion. Carrying cash, arranging a driver or fixer ahead of time, and understanding local customs round out the guidance. The overall message is to travel normally, keep one's digital footprint small, and plan for the possibility of being searched or detained.

talks.title: Preventing Zero Days, The Mandalorian Way
talks.teaser: Anders Norremo examines Preventing Zero Days, The Mandalorian Way.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, John Moeller (IT Security Manager at American Family Insurance) and Anders Norremo (founder of ThirdPartyTrust, now at BitSight) explore zero-day vulnerabilities, incident response, and third-party cyber risk management. Framing their discussion around the six cultural tenets of the Mandalorian, the speakers illustrate how foundational defense principles, cross-departmental collaboration, and supply chain awareness can protect organizations against critical vulnerabilities.

### Key Topics
- **Understanding Zero Days and the Exploit Lifecycle**: Defining a zero day as a vulnerability where defenders have had zero days to patch once known. The speakers review the progression from discovery to exploit development, black-market sales, public awareness, patch creation, and distribution.
- **The Mandalorian Framework**: Using six Mandalorian tenets to address cybersecurity practices:
  1. *Wearing Armor*: Implementing security best practices, foundational frameworks (such as the NIST Cybersecurity Framework), and solid IT asset management.
  2. *Speaking the Language*: Translating cybersecurity into the language of the business, aligning with business processes, and engaging teams during routine periods rather than only during crises.
  3. *Defending Yourself and Your Family*: Expanding security oversight beyond internal walls to cover the digital supply chain and third-party ecosystem.
  4. *Raising Children as Mandalorians*: Treating security as a shared responsibility through awareness, training, and building security guardrails.
  5. *Contributing to the Clan’s Welfare*: Sharing knowledge with suppliers, industry peers, and community groups.
  6. *Rallying to the Cause*: Cross-training teams and mobilizing the entire organization to detect and respond to security threats quickly.

### Technical Details
- **High-Profile Zero-Day and Supply Chain Incidents**: The speakers examine recent widespread events, including the 3CX Voice over IP exploit (an active supply chain breach requiring uninstallation or rapid mitigation), the SolarWinds build-system compromise affecting downstream customers, and the pervasive Log4j library vulnerability that probed an estimated 44% of corporate networks.
- **Vendor & Ecosystem Concentration**: Citing reports from Mandiant and Verizon, the speakers highlight that a significant portion of zero-day exploits (roughly 75%) concentrate around major software ecosystems—specifically Microsoft, Apple, and Google—with common threat vectors centering on credential theft, phishing, and Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP).
- **Third-Party Cyber Risk Management (TPCRM)**: Effective TPCRM requires an accurate asset inventory, assessing vendor criticality and impact, continuous monitoring, and collaborative vulnerability scanning. The speakers emphasize that third-party connections should be treated with zero trust (analogous to a hostile network) while maintaining collaborative relationships to remediate external risks.
- **Detection and Response Metrics**: While human error remains a factor in a high proportion of breaches (82% cited from Verizon data), the technical imperative is to build guardrails and automated detection. The speakers note that non-actor disclosure and detection times are increasingly measured in days rather than months.

### Takeaways
- **Asset Management is Essential**: Without deep visibility into internal software libraries and external dependencies, identifying exposure to flaws like Log4j or 3CX is nearly impossible.
- **Security Requires Cross-Functional Partnerships**: Cybersecurity teams cannot operate in a silo; success depends on embedding workflows into IT, procurement, HR, and legal operations.
- **Secure the Digital Supply Chain**: Organizations must continually monitor and assess third parties, setting clear contractual SLAs for vulnerability remediation.
- **Defense in Depth**: Organizations should apply multi-layered defenses (network segmentation, encryption, firewalls, and logging) rather than relying solely on post-release patching.

talks.title: How anyone can build their own cellular network, I built Milwaukee's - Russell From | CypherCon 6.0
talks.teaser: Covers how FCC spectrum rules and token-rewarded radio networks let individuals and small operators deploy cellular service.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a former Verizon principal telecom engineer who now runs a small company hosting cellular and IoT radios in Wisconsin, opens by explaining the push toward decentralized wireless networks. He frames the goal as sharply lower costs for mobile and home internet service, and describes how the FCC opened the 3.5 GHz CBRS band in 2020 with registration rules that anyone can follow. Federal protections for over-the-air antenna installations also let property owners and tenants put up equipment despite landlord or HOA objections.

He then walks through the current landscape. Projects such as Helium 5G and XNET pay operators in tokens based on coverage and installation quality, so a radio on a tall tower earns far more than one on a residential roof. He covers kit prices, the used-equipment market, and how deployers partner with wireless ISPs in Milwaukee and Chicago. He also reviews failures and risks, including Pollen's abrupt reversal on token value, criticism that Helium insiders did not fully disclose their holdings, thin token liquidity, and the chance that priority-access licensees could crowd out general-access users.

For anyone considering this, his advice is practical. Treat ROI calculators as optimistic and discount their estimates, favor revenue-share arrangements with building hosts over flat rent, and research a project's leadership history before buying hardware. He concludes that the radio technology works and that the main hurdle is customer adoption, so the sector remains early and speculative.

talks.title: AI for Red Team and Malware Development
talks.teaser: Shows how a red teamer uses ChatGPT and Copilot to build offensive tooling faster and get past model content filters.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how large language models and coding assistants such as ChatGPT, GitHub Copilot and Bing's chat can help red teamers write offensive tooling faster. The speaker opens with definitions of intelligence and artificial intelligence, then argues that blocking code that might be malicious would also block much legitimate software, since malware is largely ordinary code used with bad intent.

Most of the talk is a set of demonstrations. The speaker built an enumeration tool in Rust for macOS in a short session, then moved to Swift and produced several more tools, including checks for installed EDR agents from about twenty vendors. Copilot was used to generate code from inline comments in an editor. For restricted requests, a custom persona prompt worked on GPT-3.5, while GPT-4 refused a PowerShell process injection script until the request was framed as coming from a professional security researcher. A separate proof of concept had the model imagine a vulnerable network, produce plausible scan output and then walk through Metasploit steps for MS17-010. The target was fictional.

The speaker argues that machine learning defenses are still immature, with odd false positives, and that red teams should learn these tools before adversaries do. Practical advice includes splitting complex programs into API-level pieces, feeding compiler errors back to the model, and treating output as unreliable because models can hallucinate. Users should also weigh what they paste into hosted services, since prompts and code may be retained for training.

talks.title: ATT&CKing Unicorns
talks.teaser: Custom threat injections and scheduled C2 automation show whether MITRE-aligned detections still fire across Windows, Linux, and Mac.
talks.summary:
The session frames executive questions about whether security investments actually work through Eugene Spafford’s “unicorn detector” metaphor: organizations must show that controls still catch the threat actors they care about, not only on day one but continuously as technology and telemetry change.

Matt and Gary describe Northwestern Mutual’s adversarial testing workflow. They build small “threat injections” that emulate individual MITRE ATT&CK techniques, package them for repeat execution, and run them on internal Windows, Linux, and Mac images in AWS on a cron-like schedule. Beacons check into Posh C2, which queues hundreds of injections, posts outcomes to Slack for live visibility, and feeds Splunk so teams can confirm expected alerts fire—or flag “alert on alert” gaps when a rule has not triggered in hundreds of days despite a known-good test.

They argue technique IDs are too coarse when many distinct procedures exist under one sub-technique, so they document object–verb–attribute procedures in YAML, validate with Yamale, lint in GitLab CI, and orchestrate intel-to-emulation work through Jira Service Desk. Takeaways emphasize validating vendor claims, automating regression of detections and injections, and adopting a shared procedure language; they also sketch future Jinja templating and LLM-assisted generation of PowerShell threat injections from YAML.

talks.title: Hunting Before Day Zero
talks.teaser: Shows how counting low-level Linux system calls with eBPF can expose a hidden compromise and guide firewall rules.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with a firewall project for a microservice at a fast-growing software company. The service handled permissions, backed by a Redis cache and a users database, and the team needed to learn which network connections it really used before writing rules. Instead of heavyweight packet capture, they used eBPF to count TCP connection setup packets per host, which was enough to derive a safe firewall configuration.

After about a week of monitoring, the counters showed the authentication service talking far more than expected, including direct traffic to users and heavy contact with the email service. That pattern led the team to a serious problem on the host, which they were able to address. The speaker framed it as accidentally finding a zero-day. The middle of the talk compares signature-based detection, behavioral analysis and monitoring against observability, arguing that small, low-level signals such as system call counts can reveal trouble without digging through logs. Examples included tracing file access to spot unexpected reads, and a container race-condition flaw that could be detected with a one-line trace of a specific system call.

The demonstration built a process-creation counter with eBPF, exposed it to Prometheus and graphed it in Grafana, then used a test script to show a spike. The speaker noted that an attacker could flood system calls to overrun tracing buffers, though eBPF can flag that too. The takeaway is that understanding kernel fundamentals and asking precise questions of your own systems is valuable, and that the code and lab setup were shared for practice.

talks.summary:
This session walks through the most-solved challenge from a CypherCon capture-the-flag event. Only a few players completed the qualifying challenges, so the planned head-to-head final was replaced by hourly demos from the top finishers, with the challenges left open for hands-on practice. The challenge title suggested base64, but the string was not base64.

The presenter introduces CyberChef, a browser-based tool from GCHQ that runs locally and is an encoding toolkit rather than encryption. Operations are chained in a recipe, and disabling steps lets the presenter test decoders one at a time. Base58 was the only decoder that produced anything resembling text, though the output was still garbled. A hex dump showed two bytes per character, which pointed to UTF-16 little-endian, the default text encoding on Windows. The Magic operation in intensive mode then found the same result automatically.

The takeaway is that when the encoding of a string is unknown, trying common decoders in sequence and checking the character encoding can quickly reveal readable text. The presenter also notes that CyberChef is useful well beyond CTFs for hex dumps, file inspection and quick format conversions.

talks.title: When management asks you: Do you accept Agile as your lord and savior
talks.teaser: Explains how agile and lean ideas can be adapted to security operations teams, from ticket flow to metrics and alert pipelines.
talks.summary:
Daniel Lagos opens by asking whether agile can work in security operations, noting that senior leaders sometimes push teams toward it after reading popular management books. He walks through core agile principles such as delivering working increments, keeping management and staff in regular contact, and reflecting on the process at set intervals. He ties these to the theory of constraints, arguing that teams should find their bottleneck, limit work in progress and avoid taking on more alerts than analysts can handle.

The middle of the talk compares Scrum, Kanban and Scrumban by team size, roles and rules, and asks how each could fit a security operations queue. Tickets, incidents and playbooks are treated as the work product, and playbooks should run inside the ticketing system so analysts follow every step. For metrics, Lagos suggests estimating ticket effort rather than counting closures, weighting false positives differently from true positives, and using standard deviation to flag outliers.

Lagos closes by saying agile needs buy-in from both leadership and staff, and suggests regular team reviews and level workloads to prevent overload. He points to the PMI ACP certification as an entry point for project management. The Q&A covered balancing ticket assignment and how agile ideas fed into containers and Kubernetes.

Terminology shifts to “network security controls,” malware requirements embrace continuous behavioral monitoring, break-glass and shared accounts gain a compliant path, password rotation can drop when stronger account protections exist, penetration-test remediation follows the organization’s own risk standards, and broad enterprise risk assessments give way to narrower analyses. The speaker contrasts the defined implementation path with the customized approach, arguing most teams should stay on the defined route while compensating controls remain for genuine constraints.

The closing focus is on near-term work: documented scope reviews (immediate for the first 4.0 assessment), MFA for cardholder data environment access, payment-page script and tamper controls, anti-phishing for email, mandatory web application firewalls, automated security logging, monitoring critical control failures, authenticated internal vulnerability scanning ahead of 2025, and tighter definitions for scheduled activities such as quarterly scans.

talks.summary:
Jeff Man, who worked as a cryptanalyst at the NSA from 1986 to 1996, gives a historical tour of how secret communication developed. He starts with the Caesar rotation cipher and moves through substitution alphabets, the Pigpen cipher, book ciphers and transposition, with examples from the American Revolution and the Civil War. He shows how frequency analysis breaks simple substitution, and how letter counts across separate alphabets can suggest how many alphabets a message used.

The middle section covers key recovery and user error, which he argues were often how systems were actually broken. He describes a wheel he devised for U.S. Special Forces to help operators work with one-time pad tables, and notes that the Enigma machine had been broken by Polish cryptographers in the 1930s while that fact stayed secret for decades. He also covers the machine era, from half-duplex secure telephones to frequency-hopping radios, and the early move to digital encryption.

In the final part he separates codes, which operate on words and phrases, from ciphers, which operate on letters. He then outlines symmetric and public key cryptography, hashing for passwords, and protecting data at rest. He closes with quantum computing, homomorphic encryption and vendor claims about protecting data in memory, cautioning that not every new technique should be called encryption.

talks.teaser: Three VMware Horizon Log4j cases trace web shells, Cobalt Strike, miners, and EDR detection patterns.
talks.summary:
The presentation anchors on Apache Log4j’s JNDI lookup chain: malicious requests trigger LDAP fetches of Java classes that run on vulnerable servers. The speaker sketches the disclosure timeline from late 2021 through early patches, then stresses that many commercial products—especially internet-facing ones like VMware Horizon—leave defenders waiting on vendor updates rather than local configuration changes.

Three Horizon cases drive the middle of the talk. Around 23 December 2021, exploitation modified a Blast Secure Gateway JavaScript worker into a small web shell via PowerShell string insertion launched from `ws_tomcatservice.exe`, visible in PowerShell logs, process creation events, and a VM Blast Gateway service restart. A second case delivered a Cobalt Strike stager: nested Base64, XOR with decimal key 35, and C2 to an external host on ports used for staging and HTTPS beaconing; trial-license artifacts made the implant easier to spot. A third case in January 2022 dropped a Monero miner that killed rival mining processes, probed common pool ports, and persisted through scheduled tasks and run keys.

The closing material maps repeatable detection: parent `ws_tomcatservice.exe` spawning suspicious PowerShell, JNDI strings, and vendor alerts across Defender, CrowdStrike, Carbon Black, and similar platforms. Prevention emphasizes patching, WAF blocking of exploit strings, egress controls that stop secondary payload retrieval, and staying current on vendor and community threat intelligence.

He urges quarterly tuning cycles, stakeholder workshops, and measurable reduction of high-risk shares instead of infinite regex maintenance on stale policies.

talks.title: Espionage & Soviet MiGs with Dave Roebke | CypherCon 2.0
talks.teaser: Traces radar history from captured Soviet MiG training to modern jamming risks for phones, ADS-B and cars.
talks.summary:
Dave Roebke describes his earlier work supporting a US Air Force squadron that flew captured Soviet MiG fighters. The squadron trained against American F-15, F-16 and F-18 jets so pilots could see how Soviet aircraft appeared on radar. He explains radar cross section, the measure of how reflective an aircraft is to a radar beam, and notes that Soviet jets were much smaller than American ones.

He then turns to radar and radio in everyday life. Using the rotating antenna on airliners and the ADS-B system as examples, he argues that these signals can be listened to and disrupted. He explains that any frequency band can be jammed, illustrates this with cell phone frequencies, and points out that automakers use a specific microwave band for driver assistance and driverless features, which could also be jammed. He also covers line-of-sight microwave relay towers and warns that GPS satellites are vulnerable to electromagnetic pulse.

He closes by urging listeners to treat the frequency spectrum as a valuable asset, since many services depend on it. He mentions a recent report of radar being developed to detect submarine periscopes above water, and describes how modern microwave radar with phased array antennas can produce detailed, colour-coded images. The talk is a broad, anecdotal overview rather than a technical deep dive.

His intimate CypherCon session explains how polyfills keep millions of sites secure without forcing instant PHP upgrades, and where compatibility layers introduce subtle bugs or performance hits. Jacoby covers sponsorship dynamics, test matrices across versions, and why plugin authors must understand when WordPress bundles a shim versus expecting native extensions. Attendees leave with maintenance strategies for long-tail LAMP stacks common in small business footprints.

The Mandiant responder ties the hobbyist ham radio mindset to enterprise threat hunting, demonstrating aggregation pipelines that spot stalkerware, retail analytics, or rogue collectors in urban RF noise. He discusses legal boundaries, MAC randomization limits on modern phones, and why defensive teams should log passively when active scanning is impossible. Milwaukee examples ground the CypherCon talk in practical incident-response tooling.

talks.title: A Look Behind the Scenes of DEFCON DarkNet with Ed Abrams & Demetrius Comes (Part 2) | CypherCon 2.0
talks.teaser: Presenters survey classical ciphers and solve a Dark Net card puzzle built from primes, clock faces, ROT13, and a Vigenere keyword.
talks.summary:
The session assumes familiarity with the prior day’s overview of running the EC-Darknet contest at DEF CON, described as the conference’s second-largest contest after the main DEF CON contest. The presenters give a rapid history of code makers versus code breakers, from Caesar and the scytale through Mary Queen of Scots’ trial cipher, Poe’s newspaper cryptograms, and the Vigenère system cracked by Charles Babbage, tying those stories to hints embedded in their slides.

They then walk through a cipher they built for a recent Darknet quest. Gold numbers on a business card are the first twenty-six primes. Clock faces represent words encoded as little-endian base-43,200 values: each letter’s alphabet position determines how many times its corresponding prime appears in the factorization before conversion to clock notation. Working the chain reveals a URL, a trivial ROT13 payload reading “his killer,” and the answer Brutus, linking back to the Caesar material. A later segment pairs the clue Brutus with the treason trial date 15 October 1586 and uses “treason” as the Vigenère key to recover sic semper tyrannis.

They close by explaining how they aim for puzzles that are difficult yet fair—context scattered through the quest line, relatable mechanics such as base arithmetic, and heavy player collaboration, similar to broader DEF CON badge and artwork hunts. They show recent badge hardware, mention RFID and lock-picking style quests, black-badge stakes, and point attendees to dc-dark.net for an online mini-challenge before DEF CON.

talks.title: The Upside Down: Going from NetSec to AppSec with Cody Florek \ CypherCon 2.0
talks.teaser: Explains how network security teams can extend vulnerability management to web applications using pipeline-aware tooling and policy.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a common gap: a team that handles network CVEs and patching well may struggle when asked about web applications. Web application issues are catalogued as CWEs, a broad set of software design flaws whose reference material runs to around 1,500 pages, which makes it hard to turn into an operational program. Common answers such as penetration testing and manual code review are weighed for cost, repeatability, scope and training effort.

The speaker walks through the software development lifecycle, from agile delivery with frequent releases to a pipeline that carries code from a repository through build automation, containers and cloud hosting. Developers usually lack a security background and product owners set priorities, so security staff are urged to build partnerships rather than impose heavy process. Tool types are compared: static analysis of source code, dynamic testing at runtime, interactive testing that combines both, runtime agents that watch for malicious traffic, and web application firewalls as a last line that catches common injection and scripting issues.

The recommended approach is defense in depth: several tools at several layers, as much automation as possible, and CWE scans early in the build, where fixes are cheaper than in production. Network scanning should also start before go-live, with penetration testing after release and WAF and agent rules tuned over time. Policies should define acceptable vulnerabilities, remediation deadlines, what may reach production, and escalation steps.

talks.title: Explore Wisconsin Hacker History with Brad Swanson | CypherCon 2.0
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Explore Wisconsin Hacker History with Brad Swanson | CypherCon 2.0.
talks.summary:
Brad Swanson, Zendesk incident response lead in Madison, traces Wisconsin inventions and personalities that shaped hacker culture. He opens with Peter Ludlow's definition of hackers as people who repurpose familiar technology, then walks from Scholes' QWERTY typewriter through UW genetics, WHA's 9XM radio license, Bardeen and Kilby's transistor and integrated-circuit work, and Larry Landweber's CSNET backbone whose trust assumptions still haunt modern internet abuse.

People stories cover darkcode.com operator Daniel Place selling credential-stealing malware to an FBI undercover in 2010 and the Milwaukee 414s probing banks, hospitals, and Los Alamos before CFAA-era laws existed. Swanson argues the community should mentor newcomers instead of gatekeeping legitimacy and closes urging veterans to pass the torch.

talks.title: Threat Intelligence 101: Basics without Buzzwords with M4n in Bl4ck | CypherCon 2.0
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Threat Intelligence 101: Basics without Buzzwords with M4n in Bl4ck | CypherCon 2.0.
talks.summary:
The speaker billed as M4n in Black strips threat intelligence down for CypherCon newcomers. He contrasts marketing claims about real-time global feeds with a simpler definition: actionable knowledge only exists after someone else has already been harmed, so practitioners are effectively borrowing lessons from prior victims.

He walks familiar sourcing channels—government advisories, vendor feeds, ISAC communities, and STIX/TAXII sharing—then revisits Dave Bianco’s Pyramid of Pain to separate durable TTP intelligence from disposable IOCs. Using cautionary vendor blunders, he shows how uncontextualized domain or IP blocklists can take down localhost routes or block entire Yahoo CDN subdomains used by finance desks.

The core exercise transforms a shared list of scanner IPs into a story: noisy port sweeps masking Shellshock and SSH probes, with a handful of FTP attempts revealing the real entry path. He closes by urging industry ISAC participation, sane vendor automation, and visibility as the prerequisite for any feed to matter.

talks.title: JavasCrypto: How We are Using Browsers as Cryptographic Engines with Kat Traxler | CypherCon 2.0
talks.teaser: Surveys client-side browser cryptography, Web Crypto API pitfalls, and how common JavaScript libraries source randomness.
talks.summary:
Moving encryption into the browser promises users more control over data and can reduce what application operators must hold in plaintext, yet JavaScript runtimes lack strong bindings, dependency validation, protected memory, and built-in secure key storage. The talk contrasts early entropy gathering from UI events—as in the Stanford JavaScript Crypto Library—with the Web Crypto API’s push to perform cryptography and randomness outside untrusted script, typically via native hardware support.

Through a developer-style walkthrough of crypto.subtle, it shows symmetric AES key creation defaults, the extractable flag, same-origin limits, and how incorrect CORS paired with extractable keys can leak material cross-domain. A document-encryption scenario illustrates why non-extractable keys stored only in IndexedDB break when storage is cleared, pushing real designs toward wrapping keys with user-derived material and noting dangerous usage changes during unwrap. It then compares abstraction layers: event-driven “pure JavaScript” stacks, hybrid libraries such as OpenPGP.js that fall back through Node or caller-supplied buffers, and stricter Web Crypto wrappers like PKI.js that still often need shims.

Practitioners should treat browser crypto as easy to implement on paper and hard to trust in deployment: weak or mis-sourced randomness and client-side break points fail silently rather than in CI, so assessments must stress the client, not only whether the API calls look correct.

talks.title: Cluster Cracking Passwords with MDXfind & Robert Reif | CypherCon 2.0
talks.teaser: Demos a web UI for distributing hashcat cracking across many machines, and the MDXfind tool for many hash algorithms.
talks.summary:
The talk, given by a member of a hobbyist password-cracking group, looks at spreading hash cracking across many machines. The speaker presents a web front end for a cluster tool built on hashcat, where several agents, including machines that join and leave, work on one task together. Each agent enrolls with a one-time voucher, and a queue keeps results from overwhelming the database server.

A live demo uploads about 4,000 MD5 hashes, then creates a brute-force task and a wordlist-with-rules task, showing chunking, priorities, preconfigured tasks and super tasks. Zaps, which share cracks across all agents, keep every machine current, which matters for salted hashes. Limits include no support for increment or mask files, and macOS needs hashcat built by hand. Every client also receives all cracked hashes and wordlists, so client machines must be trusted.

The second half covers MDXfind, a tool begun in 2013 to iterate MD5 that now supports almost 500 algorithms, including nested combinations. It handles very long hashes and lists of tens of millions of entries with little slowdown, and can run many hash types against one dictionary in a single pass. The speaker shows how to identify an unknown 32-character hex hash by letting the tool test candidate algorithms, and says MDXfind complements hashcat rather than replacing it.

talks.title: Badge Panel | CypherCon 2.0
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Badge Panel | CypherCon 2.0.
talks.summary:
### Overview
At CypherCon 2.0, a panel of six electronic badge creators discussed the technical and logistical realities of the "#badgelife" culture. The discussion covered hardware design trade-offs, microcontroller choices, protocol implementations, firmware development challenges, and the intense effort required to build, hand-assemble, and debug custom interactive conference badges.

### Key Topics
- **Power Management & Switches:** The panel addressed why many badges omit hardware power switches. Surface-mount technology (SMT) switches frequently tear off or lift PCB pads when bumped. Some creators rely on standby sleep modes, software switching, or capacitive touch, while one team engineered a dual-button setup where a hardware switch bootstraps the regulator and software takes over to reduce standby current to 6 µA.
- **Component Selection & Sourcing:** Component choice is primarily governed by cost, existing libraries, and availability. Sourcing surprises are common; one team experienced electrical noise issues with IrDA transceiver batches, while another had to hand-solder thousands of LEDs after lead-free reflow oven temperatures cracked APA102 LED packages. Sourcing parts early from overseas brokers before locking board layouts is critical.
- **LED Protocols & Drivers:** The panelists debated addressable LED protocols. APA102 LEDs were praised for their separate hardware SPI clock line, enabling high data transfer rates and asynchronous transmission via DMA without bit-banging. In contrast, WS2812B LEDs require tight, strict timing, presenting challenges on 8-bit microcontrollers and specific MCU platforms like Nordic (due to 255-byte DMA packet limits), requiring circular buffers or assembly-level tuning.
- **Assembly and Physical Constraints:** Panelists highlighted assembly constraints when building hundreds to thousands of boards. Constraints include avoiding QFNs, sticking to SOIC/QFP footprints, and choosing passive component sizes no smaller than 0603 to ensure manual placement with tweezers and stencils is feasible.
- **Firmware Architecture & Memory Optimization:** Teams shared strategies for overcoming extreme memory limitations. One badge used two microcontrollers (a Microchip PIC and a Parallax Propeller). When Propeller code space ran out, strings were offloaded into the PIC's EEPROM, freeing memory for features like a custom text adventure, an operating system, and frequency generation for DTMF and phreaking modes.
- **Interactivity and Easter Eggs:** The panel traced the evolution from simple static/blinking boards to interactive network nodes. Badges integrated peer-to-peer relaying, IrDA communication, telnet-style multi-hop chat, hidden Easter eggs (like silos and maze puzzles), and embedded games (such as Chip-8 emulators, Flappy Bird, and wireless multiplayer games).

### Technical Details
- **Microcontrollers & Architectures:** Implementations discussed include Atmel XMega (hardware SPI and DMA), Microchip PIC (hardware IrDA SIR mode, assembly and C), Nordic MCUs, and the multi-core Parallax Propeller (programmed in Spin).
- **Infrared & Communication Protocols:** IrDA SIR (Simple IR) mode acts as a glorified UART, pulsing high once every bit-time divided by 8 to sync and reject reflections. Other discussions noted repurposing badges for IR remote manipulation (TV-B-Gone style) and Bluetooth trolling.
- **PCB Design:** One team highlighted designing multi-sided 3D cube badges with complex trace routing and zero vias on the outer faces.

### Takeaways
Badge engineering requires balancing ambition with harsh physical and manufacturing realities. Builders must navigate component fragility, supply-chain variability, strict reflow profiles, and tight memory limits while writing regression-tested firmware under fixed conference deadlines.

talks.title: Protecting Passwords with Oblivious Cryptography with Adam Everspaugh | CypherCon 2.0
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Protecting Passwords with Oblivious Cryptography with Adam Everspaugh | CypherCon 2.0.
talks.summary:
Adam Everspaugh presents Pythia, a partially oblivious PRF service that lets web servers outsource password hashing to hardened crypto servers using blinded bilinear-pairing requests. Clients never hold master secrets locally, can detect online guessing tied to user IDs, and rotate keys after breaches to cryptographically erase stolen databases without forcing users to pick new passwords.

The design extends Facebook’s split HMAC architecture, supports multi-tenant APIs, and ships an open-source nginx reference achieving single-digit millisecond latency versus costly on-box iteration. He contrasts leaky historical breaches, sketches Bitcoin brain-wallet and remote file-encryption scenarios, and invites operators to run Pythia alongside bcrypt rather than treating static hashes as sufficient after large credential dumps leak.. Q&A covers consumer deployments, denial-of-service risks during key rotation, and bilinear curve choices in the open-source nginx prototype.

talks.title: The History of Video Game Console Hacking with Dan Loosen | CypherCon 2.0
talks.teaser: Spans homebrew console scenes, famous reverse-engineering lawsuits, and hard lessons from pressing independent Dreamcast games.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with how the speaker’s retro retail venture, community festivals, and a Midwest Gaming Classic demo disc led into publishing independent Dreamcast software built on Dan Potter’s Chaos development environment. Feet of Fury became an early post-shutdown physical release, followed by coding contests that produced titles such as Inhabitants and Maqupai.

The middle of the talk weaves that publishing story with a plain-language tour of landmark console litigation: Activision versus Atari, Coleco’s expansion adapter, Tengen’s misappropriated Nintendo lockout secrets, Accolade’s lawful Sega Genesis reverse engineering victory, and Sony’s repeated suits against Bleem. When a batch of pressed Dreamcast discs failed to boot, manufacturers cited DMCA risk; months of legal homework were needed before replacements could ship.

Later sections cover hardware assists such as the Jaguar Skunk Board flash cartridge, ongoing struggles shipping Jay Townsend’s Slave when emulation diverged from real hardware, MIL-CD compatibility myths, and the shrinking economics of physical retro releases. Q&A clarifies that retail Dreamcast units still run MIL-CD style independent discs and why the shop stayed focused on consoles instead of PC ports.

talks.title: Wireless Hacking & Capture the Flag with Eric Escobar | CypherCon 2.0
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Wireless Hacking & Capture the Flag with Eric Escobar | CypherCon 2.0.
talks.summary:
### Overview
At CypherCon 2.0, Eric Escobar of SecureWorks presents an introductory talk on software-defined radio (SDR) and wireless replay attacks, previewing challenges designed for the conference's Wireless Capture the Flag (CTF). Escobar explains that many cheap commercial electronic devices—particularly those operating around 433–434 MHz—lack encryption or rolling-code protections, making them inherently vulnerable to signal capture and replay attacks.

### Key Concepts & Hardware
Escobar outlines fundamental concepts required for RF analysis:
- **Duplexity**: Differentiating half-duplex systems (listen or talk one at a time, like walkie-talkies) from full-duplex systems (simultaneous transmit and receive, like telephones).
- **Sampling Rates**: Measured in million samples per second (MSPS), balancing between sufficient sample resolution to capture signals accurately without overloading computer processors or draining battery.
- **SDR Hardware Options**: Ranging from inexpensive $20 RTL-SDR TV tuners (receive-only with broad range), to intermediate transceivers like the Yard Stick One ($115, half-duplex), up to higher-end full-duplex transceivers such as the BladeRF ($650) with temperature-stabilized oscillators.

### Technical Details & Tooling
To inspect unknown devices without manually decoding signals from raw waterfall plots, Escobar recommends looking up the device's FCC ID via `fcc.io` to retrieve public filings, internal photos, frequencies, and modulation specs. Many cheap devices rely on amplitude modulation (AM) via On-Off Keying (OOK), encoding binary ones and zeros as high/low signal pulses and repeatedly retransmitting packets to survive RF interference.

Signal analysis and exploitation tools highlighted include:
- **Audacity**: Audio editor used to inspect `.wav` or raw signal captures visually and measure bit timings.
- **GNU Radio & GQRX**: Popular open-source SDR toolkits for Unix systems.
- **SDR# (SDRSharp)**: Windows-based platform capable of tasks such as tracking unencrypted aircraft beacons.
- **RFcat**: Python-driven framework for RF manipulation.
- **OOKtools**: Specialized software for scanning frequencies, identifying baud rates, and demodulating OOK signals (primarily with the Yard Stick One).
- **HackRF Tools**: Demonstrating straightforward capture and replay using the `hackrf_transfer` command-line utility at specified frequencies (e.g., 434 MHz).

### Target Vulnerabilities & CTF Preview
Escobar presents practical demonstrations of replay attacks against consumer hardware, including battery-deprived motion detectors, wireless doorbells, sequentially triggered Etekcity wireless power outlets, automated gated-community barriers, and an unencrypted dog shock collar. The presentation concludes with logistics for the CypherCon Wireless CTF (`CypherCon_WCTF`), which features fox hunts, ham radio number stations, SDR replay stations, and war driving verification against 7,500 mapped points in Milwaukee.

talks.title: Brain Based Authentication with Melanie Segado & Sydney Swaine-Simon | CypherCon 2.0
talks.teaser: Surveys brain-wave biometrics and BCIs, argues against deploying EEG login today, and warns about insecure consumer headsets.
talks.summary:
The session opens with NeuroTechX and a tour of neurotechnology—from MRI and transcranial stimulation to EEG as a practical, increasingly affordable way to read brain activity. It frames brain-based authentication as a growing research area, walking through the brain–computer interface loop (signal acquisition, feature extraction, classifiers, and feedback) and the two signal families most used for identification: event-related potentials such as P300 spellers and resting-state neural oscillations, where published work reports very high identification rates under controlled conditions.

The core argument is that EEG biometrics are a poor choice for protecting homes or workplaces today. Measured against standard biometric criteria—universality, uniqueness, permanence, measurability, performance, acceptability, and circumvention—the speaker highlights fatigue, injury, headset quality, and environmental noise as showstoppers, while noting that modality switching and steady-state visual evoked potentials can help with liveness. Consumer EEG hardware is often treated as IoT without serious security, leaving room for man-in-the-middle abuse, and crowdfunding devices are cautioned against as unsupported hype.

For practitioners who still want to experiment, the talk recommends layered authentication, rigorous protocols, and collaboration with neuroscience researchers. It recounts a rushed acronym-based ERP trial that failed despite expensive gear and shielding, then points to open databases, MNE, PsychoPy, OpenBCI, and community resources for hands-on learning. Closing Q&A reinforces deleting templates after brain injury, long timelines to marketplace readiness, electrode placement constraints, and limits for neurodegenerative conditions.

talks.title: Hypervault Demo & HTTP and SSH Tunneling with Caleb Madrigal | CypherCon 1.0
talks.teaser: Covers a browser-based file vault demo and practical HTTP, SSH, and DNS tunneling past restrictive proxies and firewalls.
talks.summary:
The session opens with Hypervault, a static, self-contained HTML file-encryption web application that needs no install or network access once saved. The demo walks through dragging files or inline text into the vault, setting a password with scrypt-based key derivation, and downloading a single “locked vault” HTML file that embeds both encrypted payloads and the decryption code so the bundle stays usable even if the upstream project disappears.

The presenter explains that Hypervault targets data at rest, not transit, because a man-in-the-middle could swap the embedded JavaScript unless recipients verify integrity out of band. Implementation details include the TripleSec library stacking multiple ciphers, browser sandboxing, and zero server-side knowledge. Brief Q&A notes limited mobile creation support and HTML5 dependencies.

The second segment defines protocol tunneling and contrasts routine encapsulation with deliberately hiding traffic inside allowed protocols. HTTP tunneling covers CONNECT proxies versus encoding data in valid HTTP (including a minimal “prepend a header” trick used against deep packet inspection). SSH tunneling demonstrates a local SOCKS proxy via ssh -D, with a live curl example showing egress through the remote host’s IP and limits on encryption only to the SSH hop. DNS tunneling introduces iodine for environments that permit outbound DNS, an airplane captive-portal experiment, Wireshark observations, reliability quirks across client versions, and pointers to a personal setup guide.

talks.title: Bypassing Encryption by Attacking the Cryptosystem Perimeter w/Trenton Ivey | CypherCon 1.0
talks.teaser: Demonstrates perimeter attacks that steal keys and passwords from browsers, disk tools, and vault apps without breaking the crypto.
talks.summary:
The presentation reframes encryption security around Alice, Bob, Eve, Mallory, and a red-team figure who already sits on endpoints where keys and plaintext live. Rather than attacking algorithms, it chains quick demonstrations that abuse process memory, API calls, and trojanized tooling.

On Linux, a Firefox login over HTTPS still leaves credentials recoverable from a gcore dump after the tab closes. On Windows, Procmon and Immunity Debugger trace VeraCrypt’s use of GetWindowTextW; MinHook and a reflective DLL log the volume password while mounting succeeds. A PATH-prepended sudo wrapper, a rebuilt OpenSSH client that logs passphrases, and a patched KeePassX DLL-load issue show credential theft and even remote DLL placement on a shared vault folder leading to shell access. A Hypervault walkthrough adds JavaScript to an exported file so a decrypt hook exfiltrates the passphrase via a crafted image request.

Closing guidance stresses endpoint hardening alongside crypto design: shorten credential lifetime in memory where possible, assume compromised hosts when threat modeling, and use integrity monitoring so clients like SSH or Keeps aren’t silently replaced. VeraCrypt’s immediate password zeroing is held up as a bar others can emulate.

talks.title: PISSED: Privacy In a Surveillance State, Evading Detection with Joe Cicero | CypherCon 1.0
talks.teaser: Shows how people who thought they were anonymous online were unmasked through logs, metadata, writing style and mistakes.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a story about a LinkedIn contact whose claims did not check out, and how the speaker looked into the stated employer, location and education to expose the inconsistencies. It then argues that surveillance has grown since the Carnivore era and that records shared with third parties are easier for authorities to reach. Everyday reasons for anonymity follow, including a disputed online review, a traveller detained over a social media post, and bloggers facing danger.

The middle section covers how people were identified despite believing they were anonymous. A man who publicised a flaw he had accessed was arrested, and a teenager running a denial-of-service attack from home was traced. Writing-style tools can attribute prose, while server logs, network addresses and hotel Wi-Fi records linked activity to individuals in other cases. A bomb threat sent through Tor was traced by checking which machine was using the network at that time.

The speaker also questions how far anonymity tools can be trusted, citing a tool that reported real locations and Tor exit nodes that can see unencrypted traffic. The takeaway is that software can fail, any single operational slip can expose you, and the cost of one mistake may be high. Avoid reusing networks or locations, and prefer read-only systems.

talks.title: Curry and TARTS with JP SMITH | CypherCon 1.0
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Curry and TARTS with JP SMITH | CypherCon 1.0.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk presented at CypherCon 1.0, JP Smith discusses the fundamental challenge of reasoning about software behavior and guaranteeing correctness. While software behaves one way in a developer's mind or during testing, real-world execution on production hardware can behave very differently. Using side-channel timing attacks as a prime motivating example, Smith explores how conventional testing methodologies fall short and presents formal verification through dependently typed programming languages as an alternative method to mathematically prove code security properties.

### Key Topics
- **The Problem of Program Reasoning**: Discrepancies between theoretical code design, developer intent, development environments, and actual production behavior.
- **Side-Channel Timing Attacks**: How non-functional execution details (time, power, CPU operations) expose vulnerabilities in cryptosystems even when mathematical encryption cannot be directly reversed.
- **Limitations of Traditional Assurance**: Why code review, unit testing, property-based testing, and fuzzing fail to guarantee security across all possible input domains.
- **Type Systems as Logical Propositions**: The concept that types represent propositions and program terms represent proofs, which compilers verify.
- **Dependent Types and Proof Assistants**: Applying languages like Idris, Agda, and Coq to encode and formally verify complex properties, including constant-time cryptographic operations.

### Technical Details
Smith illustrates timing attacks using a naive byte equality function that loops bit by bit and stops early on the first mismatch. Comparing bytes that differ only at the end takes more loop iterations and time than comparing bytes that differ at the first bit. An attacker querying a password checker can evaluate response times to reveal each bit successively in O(n) time, effectively executing a binary search over secret data. Smith cites historical milestones where timing attacks broke production cryptosystems:
- In 1999, Kocher broke RSA.
- In 2003, Boneh and Brumley broke SSL.
- In 2005, timing attacks broke AES.

Traditional testing covers only a subset of potential inputs and assumes malicious actors will not uncover degenerate paths. In contrast, formal verification leverages type systems where propositions correspond to types and functions serve as proofs. In dependently typed languages (such as Idris, Agda, and Coq), types can depend on values, allowing programmers to formulate arbitrary propositions—from the Pythagorean theorem to runtime guarantees. 

Smith demonstrates modeling an equality function returning both a boolean bit and an operation counter (a natural number representing execution time). By formulating a dependent type stating that for any bytes `a, b, c, d`, the time to compare `(a, b)` equals the time to compare `(c, d)`, the compiler can verify that the comparison runs in constant time across all inputs, mathematically ruling out timing-based side channels.

### Takeaways
- Standard testing only asserts that software works in tested scenarios, which provides insufficient protection against adversarial exploitation.
- Dependently typed languages enable developers to turn code verification into proof checking, ensuring properties hold for all inputs rather than a sampled set.
- While formal proof techniques provide absolute guarantees, Smith cautions that current tooling (Idris, Agda, Coq) primarily resides in academia and is not ready for mainstream production deployments.
- Shifting security mindsets from "we tried hard to break it and failed" to "we proved it cannot break under any circumstances" offers a powerful theoretical direction for high-assurance software.

talks.title: No Encrypted Data on This Drive; Just Pictures of My Cat with Parker Schmitt | CypherCon 1.0
talks.teaser: Explores steganography and one-time-pad deniability so mundane files can conceal secrets and resist coerced key disclosure.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens from a provocative premise: investigators expect obvious ciphertext, while ordinary media such as cat pictures can carry hidden material that is hard to spot and easy to deny. It frames the rubber-hose problem—physical or legal coercion to recover keys—and links that pressure to forced key escrow debates, including high-profile fights over device encryption.

The core journey contrasts hiding from machines versus humans: classic least-significant-bit image stego fails once anyone knows to look, while whitespace encoders, RFC-shaped traffic, and innocent attachments can move bytes out of band without tripping typical inspection. The speaker treats the one-time pad as the ideal hiding primitive—XOR can make any file statistically ambiguous—and then sketches a more practical scheme: embed key material at scattered byte positions, derive access paths from passwords via number-theoretic sequences (primes, primitive roots, cyclic indexing), and optionally layer stream ciphers such as Salsa20 or AES. Larger carriers increase combinatorial obscurity; junk bytes may represent yet another latent message.

The closing operational picture is three unlockable plaintexts: a harmless cover, a believable but embarrassing decoy, and the true payload—so an interrogator may stop after apparent success. The talk is an accelerated design overview with little live demonstration, aimed at practitioners thinking about plausible deniability rather than product-grade implementations.

talks.title: Security Control Wins & Fails with Jason Lang | CypherCon 1.0
talks.teaser: Ranks common security controls as wins or fails based on how well they slow down a determined intruder.
talks.summary:
A penetration tester gives an attacker's view of ten common security controls, sorting each into a win or fail column based on whether it actually slows down a determined intruder. He stresses that the ratings reflect his own experience, that a control that fails against him may still work against other threats, and that the goal is to help defenders decide where to spend limited money and time.

The wins include network access control, which stops unauthorized devices at the switch port, and network segmentation, which separates domain controllers, database servers and mail servers so that only specific jump boxes can reach them. He also rates ongoing security awareness training as a win when it uses realistic phishing exercises rather than click-through computer-based courses. Privileged account management, including removing admin rights once they are no longer needed, and free Active Directory Group Policy settings such as NTLMv2 and SMB signing also count as wins.

The fails include antivirus that ignores PowerShell, which is rarely blocked and can be evaded with packed binaries, and data loss prevention that watches email but not data copied out over a remote desktop session. Unenforced security policies, intrusion detection left in audit mode or with alerts nobody follows up on, and most newly purchased tools also land in the fail column. He closes by urging defenders to hire good people and use the tools they already own.
